stories.headline: IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI STRIKES ON SAUDI OIL FACILITIES SEND BRENT NEAR $99, RATTLING STOCKS
stories.body: Iran-aligned Houthi militants claimed responsibility for strikes that halted operations at multiple Saudi Arabian energy facilities Tuesday, pushing Brent crude to an intraday high of $99.46 a barrel — its highest since July — as the months-long U.S.-Iran tanker conflict in the Strait of Hormuz widens to a third Gulf player. Brent settled near $98 and WTI topped $92.90, with the risk premium spilling directly into U.S. equities as energy-sensitive and rate-sensitive sectors led the S&P 500 lower.
stories.explain: Saudi Arabia is the swing producer OPEC+ leans on to backfill lost barrels during a supply shock, so an attack on its own export infrastructure removes the market's usual shock absorber at the worst possible moment. That's why oil reacted more sharply to this strike than to earlier Hormuz skirmishes alone — traders are now pricing the risk that the conflict spreads beyond Iranian shipping into the Gulf's core production capacity.

stories.headline: DOW SHEDS 628 POINTS AS OIL SPIKE, CANADA TARIFFS AND STICKY YIELDS COLLIDE
stories.body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 628.18 points (-1.18%) to 52,786.07, the S&P 500 slid 0.58% to 7,675.28, and the Nasdaq Composite eased 0.32% to 26,421.41 as investors absorbed rising oil prices, escalating Mideast conflict, and Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods, which took effect just after midnight. Apple (-2.55%), Alphabet (-2.10%) and Microsoft (-2.05%) led mega-cap tech lower, while Caterpillar (+1.65%) and Honeywell (+0.95%) outperformed.
stories.explain: Tuesday's selloff wasn't one shock but four compounding at once: expensive oil threatens to reignite inflation, strong recent jobs data gives the Fed less room to look past that inflation, rising Treasury yields raise the discount rate applied to future earnings, and new tariffs add a fresh cost shock on top of all three. When several negative catalysts land in the same session, index-level moves tend to overstate any single story's importance — which is why Wednesday's price action will say more about which of these four actually sticks.

stories.headline: WTI TOPS $92.90, BRENT NEARS $99 AS CRUDE EXTENDS AN 8%+ SEPTEMBER SURGE
stories.body: WTI crude climbed 1.6% to $92.90 a barrel and Brent pushed toward $98-99 after touching an intraday high of $99.46, extending a more than 8% gain for crude so far in September as the U.S.-Iran tanker war widens. Since September 1, U.S. strikes have disabled or destroyed five Iranian-flagged tankers under a new 'tanker-for-tanker' retaliation policy, while Tuesday's Houthi strikes on Saudi facilities mark the first direct hit on Gulf production infrastructure this cycle.
stories.explain: A barrel of WTI trading above $90 for a sustained stretch typically adds noticeably to headline CPI within one to two months, both directly through gasoline prices and indirectly through higher shipping and input costs economy-wide. With CPI due Friday, September 11 and the Fed's rate decision the following week, this move couldn't land at a more sensitive point in the data calendar.

stories.headline: CANADA'S RETALIATORY TARIFFS ON U.S. GOODS TAKE EFFECT AS TRADE TALKS COLLAPSE
stories.body: Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect just after midnight Tuesday after Prime Minister Mark Carney escalated economic pressure on America's largest trading partner following the breakdown of negotiations last month, adding a fresh cross-border cost shock on top of an already volatile session driven by oil and Mideast risk.
stories.explain: Retaliatory tariffs function as a tax both sides' consumers ultimately share: Canadian duties raise costs for U.S. exporters trying to sell into that market, while reciprocal U.S. tariffs already in place raise costs for American importers and, eventually, American shoppers. The market impact shows up less in a single day's index move and more in guidance cuts from companies with heavy cross-border supply chains over the following weeks.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD PUSHES TOWARD 4.81%, NEARING A LEVEL ANALYSTS CALL A RISK-ASSET TRIPWIRE
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to roughly 4.81% Tuesday, edging closer to the 4.8% threshold that market analysts warn could create 'meaningful problems' for other asset classes if breached on a sustained basis. The move comes five days before Friday's CPI print and just over a week before the Fed's September 15-16 FOMC meeting, where rate-decision odds remain split between a hold and a 25 bp hike.
stories.explain: Above roughly 4.8%, the 10-year yield starts competing more aggressively with equities for capital, since it offers a risk-free return closer to what stocks have historically delivered on average. Rising yields also raise the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows, which hits high-multiple growth and tech stocks hardest — exactly the group leading Tuesday's decline.

stories.headline: DUKE TOPS ANDY KATZ'S FIRST MEN'S BASKETBALL POWER 44 FOR 2026-27 SEASON
stories.body: Six weeks before tip-off, ESPN's Andy Katz released his first men's college basketball Power 44 rankings and bracket predictions for 2026-27, slotting Duke at No. 1 as coverage shifts from portal and recruiting moves toward season previews. Most programs open practice in October with non-conference schedules still being finalized.

stories.headline: NBA STRIPS CLIPPERS OF FIVE FIRST-ROUND PICKS, FINES BALLMER $30 MILLION IN KAWHI LEONARD CAP PROBE
stories.body: The NBA concluded its investigation into alleged salary-cap circumvention tied to Kawhi Leonard's since-completed move away from the Clippers, stripping Los Angeles of five first-round draft picks and fining owner Steve Ballmer $30 million — one of the league's harshest cap-related penalties on record.

stories.headline: PATRIOTS SIGN CB CHRISTIAN GONZALEZ TO 4-YEAR, $135M EXTENSION AHEAD OF SEAHAWKS OPENER
stories.body: New England locked up cornerback Christian Gonzalez on a four-year, $135 million extension one day before Wednesday's NFL Kickoff Game at Seattle — a Super Bowl LX rematch after the Seahawks beat the Patriots 29-13 in February. Kickoff is 5:20 PM PT on NBC.

stories.headline: SEC LOOKS INTO LSU AFTER LANE KIFFIN SIGNS PLAYERS CUT FROM NFL CAMPS
stories.body: The SEC is reviewing LSU's roster-building tactics, including the program's conference standing, after coach Lane Kiffin signed several players recently cut from NFL training camp rosters — a legal but conference-rattling maneuver that came days after LSU's 51-10 Week 1 rout of Clemson vaulted the Tigers up national power rankings.

sports.detail: No. 17 Washington beat Washington State 24-10 in the 118th Apple Cup Sunday at Husky Stadium; Demond Williams Jr. threw for 268 yards and a touchdown and added a rushing score. Huskies host Utah State next, Saturday, Sept. 12, 12:30 PM PT on BTN.

Texas Tech transfer LeJuan Watts (11.8 pts, 6.0 reb last season) and guard Harun Zrno continue building out coach Danny Sprinkle's roster. Washington added a road exhibition at Boise State on Oct. 17 before hosting rival Washington State on Oct. 25.

The defending Super Bowl LX champs host New England in Wednesday's NFL Kickoff Game (5:20 PM PT, NBC) at Lumen Field — a rematch of Seattle's 29-13 title-game win. The Patriots enter having just signed CB Christian Gonzalez to a 4-year, $135M extension.

Jalen Duren's restricted free agency standoff drags into September — Detroit's five-year, ~$35M/year offer remains roughly $5M annually below the All-NBA center's ask. Duren could play on his $9.6M qualifying offer and reach unrestricted free agency next summer. Season opens at Boston, Tuesday, Oct. 20.

Seattle (67-77, 3rd in the AL West) opens a three-game homestand against Texas Tuesday night at T-Mobile Park (6:40 PM MT), a step back from last year's AL West title as the regular season winds down toward its Sept. 27 finale.

watchlist: CPI data Friday, Sept. 11, 8:30 AM ET — first real read on how oil's spike above $90 WTI is feeding into headline inflation
FOMC meeting Sept. 15-16 — rate decision Wednesday, Sept. 16 at 2:00 PM ET with hike/hold odds still split
10-year Treasury yield near 4.81% — a sustained break above 4.8% is the level analysts are flagging as a risk-asset tripwire
Seahawks host Patriots in the NFL Kickoff Game — Wednesday, Sept. 9, 5:20 PM PT, Lumen Field, Super Bowl LX rematch
Mariners host Rangers — Tuesday, Sept. 8, T-Mobile Park, opening a season-closing homestand

deepDive.title: Oil at $99, Yields at 4.81%: How a Supply Shock Becomes a Fed Problem
content: Two numbers defined Tuesday's session: Brent crude touching $99.46 after Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities, and the 10-year Treasury yield pushing toward 4.81%, a level analysts are flagging as a threshold that could strain other asset classes. These aren't separate stories — they're the same story viewed from two markets. An oil shock five days before a CPI print and just over a week before an FOMC decision doesn't just move gas prices; it moves the market's entire read on where the Fed's reaction function is headed, and that read shows up first in the bond market.

The mechanism runs through the CPI basket and the term premium. Energy carries roughly a 7% direct weight in headline CPI, and a sustained move above $90 WTI typically shows up in gasoline and utility prices within four to eight weeks, plus a slower indirect drag through transportation and input costs across nearly every other category. When traders expect that inflation path to run hotter, they demand more compensation for holding longer-dated bonds — the 'term premium' — which pushes the 10-year yield higher independent of what the Fed does with its overnight rate target.

What's easy to miss is that the Fed doesn't automatically react to supply-shock inflation the way it does to demand-driven inflation — in theory. During the 1990 Gulf War oil shock and again after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine sent CPI to 9.1%, policymakers initially tried to distinguish a one-time price-level shift from a lasting inflation problem. In practice, both episodes forced the Fed's hand anyway, because a shock large enough or persistent enough starts shifting the public's inflation expectations — and once expectations de-anchor, the 'look through it' option disappears and rate hikes follow regardless of the shock's origin.

That's the lens for the next ten days. Friday's CPI print will show how much of this oil move has already passed through, but the more important number to watch is what happens to inflation expectations — breakevens and survey data — not the headline print itself. If expectations stay anchored, the Fed has room to treat this as noise heading into the September 15-16 meeting, consistent with rate-decision odds still sitting near a coin flip. If they don't, a hold becomes much harder to justify, and Tuesday's 4.81% could look like the early edge of a bigger move rather than a ceiling.
